ov: Not a crab at all but a relative of spiders and scorpions, little changed for about 250 million years. Four species survive: one on the Atlantic coast of the US and Mexico, and three in South, Southeast and East Asia. It lives on the seabed but can swim, and comes ashore to spawn.

why.et: Eaten as a delicacy in parts of Asia; in the United States it is caught for fishing bait and for its blood.

len: Up to 79.5 cm with the tail (tri-spine horseshoe crab)
rg: The Atlantic coast of the United States and the Gulf of Mexico, plus coasts of South, Southeast and East Asia.
df: Worms, clams and other molluscs on the seabed, and sometimes crustaceans and small fish. It forages mostly at night.

cf.tip: Despite its name it is not a crab or even a crustacean: it is a chelicerate, more closely related to spiders, ticks and scorpions.

fx: Its blood is blue because it carries oxygen with copper-based hemocyanin instead of iron-based haemoglobin.
Its eyes are a million times more sensitive to light at night than during the day.
